overview: The Parents Opt-in Protection Act changes a federal law that protects students' privacy in schools that receive federal education funding. Under current law, students cannot be required to take part in surveys, analyses or evaluations that ask about sensitive topics, such as political beliefs, mental health, sexual behavior, religion or family income, without consent. This bill requires that consent to be in writing and given separately for each specific survey, from the student if they are an adult or emancipated minor, or from a parent otherwise. It applies the same written, survey-by-survey consent rule to certain surveys funded by outside parties. As of September 24, 2026, a House committee had approved an amended version and it was awaiting action by the full House.
for: Supporters say parents should have to actively agree, in writing, before their children are asked personal questions, rather than having to find out and object after the fact.
against: Critics say requiring separate written consent for every survey adds paperwork for schools and could lower participation in surveys that help identify student health and safety needs.
